findings.title: Pin and verify the downloaded installer before executing it
findings.whyItBreaks: Every image build fetches mutable network content and pipes it directly to sh. A compromised endpoint, DNS/proxy interception, or changed installer can execute arbitrary code in the build environment and silently alter the produced image.

findings.title: Pin and verify the downloaded installer before executing it
findings.whyItBreaks: This executes whatever bytes https://example.com/install.sh serves at build time, without a version pin, checksum, or signature verification. A compromised, changed, or redirected endpoint gains arbitrary code execution in the image build and can alter the shipped image.

findings.title: Fail the build when the installer download fails
findings.whyItBreaks: Without curl --fail and pipefail, a network-level curl failure feeds an empty stream to sh; sh exits successfully, so Docker can produce an image without the intended installation. The failure is indistinguishable from a successful install.

findings.title: Pin and verify the installer before executing it
findings.whyItBreaks: This executes whatever bytes the remote URL serves at build time. A compromised origin, DNS/TLS interception, or later change to the script can inject arbitrary commands into the build image and makes builds non-reproducible.

findings.title: Preserve the missing-key error
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing for an absent key at src/store.go:10, but this public helper discards that signal and returns "", which is also the valid value for a present key mapped to an empty string. Callers cannot distinguish lookup failure from a real empty value.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key failures in LoadOrDefault
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing for an absent key, but this public function discards that error and returns "". Callers cannot distinguish a missing key from a present key whose valid value is empty.

findings.title: Preserve the missing-key error in the public wrapper
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing for an absent key, but this exported API discards it and returns "", which is also a valid stored map value. Callers cannot distinguish absent data from an explicitly empty value.

findings.title: Preserve Run's completion-before-return behavior
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously Run returned only after every result had been sent. It now launches sends and returns immediately. A caller that closes the results channel after Run returns can race with these goroutines and panic with "send on closed channel"; consumers can also observe incomplete results at return.

findings.title: Require an administrator before authorizing deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: With a session where isAdmin=false and tenantId matches the record, this now returns true, allowing any tenant member to delete records despite not being an administrator. It also authorizes an administrator against a record from another tenant.

findings.title: Require both tenant membership and admin status
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing && to || authorizes a non-admin whenever their tenant matches the record, and authorizes an admin from any tenant. The prior policy required both conditions, so this permits cross-tenant or non-admin record deletion.

findings.title: Require both admin status and tenant match
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing && to || authorizes a non-admin for any record in their tenant, and authorizes an admin for records in other tenants. Both paths were denied before and bypass the intended tenant-scoped admin check.

findings.title: Preserve parse failures instead of overwriting settings
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid JSON or an invalid settings shape previously threw before updateFontSize could save. It now becomes DEFAULTS; updateFontSize then changes only fontSize and persists it, silently replacing the user's existing theme/settings with {"theme":"light","fontSize":size}.

findings.title: Preserve parse failures when updating settings
findings.whyItBreaks: A malformed or schema-invalid stored value now becomes DEFAULTS. updateFontSize then changes that fallback and saves it, overwriting the user's original settings instead of surfacing the parse error. For example, invalid JSON is converted to {"theme":"light","fontSize":<size>} at line 22.

findings.title: Propagate invalid-settings errors instead of defaulting
findings.whyItBreaks: JSON or schema validation failures previously stopped callers. They now return the real-looking default settings. updateFontSize then sets only fontSize and saves them, so input such as {"theme":"dark"} silently becomes {"theme":"light","fontSize":16}, overwriting the user's valid theme.

findings.whyItBreaks: For a non-zero remainder, floor division undercounts pages: pageCount(1, 10) returns 0 and pageCount(11, 10) returns 1, so consumers omit the page containing remaining items.

findings.title: Return artifacts for the reported branch
findings.whyItBreaks: For any branch other than "verified", builtFrom is the branch commit but artifacts are fetched from the unrelated verified ref. The report therefore misattributes verified artifacts to the requested branch.

findings.title: Load artifacts from the reported commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any branch whose ref differs from "verified", builtFrom contains build.ref(branch) but artifacts contain build.artifactsAt(build.ref("verified")). Consumers receive a self-inconsistent report and can associate verified artifacts with the wrong branch commit.

findings.title: Fetch artifacts from the requested branch commit
findings.whyItBreaks: When build.ref(branch) and build.ref("verified") differ, the report returns builtFrom as the branch commit but obtains artifacts from the verified commit. Consumers receive internally inconsistent report data and can publish or inspect artifacts for the wrong revision.

findings.title: Restore slicing to enforce the requested limit
findings.whyItBreaks: For every positive limit, the function now returns all entries instead of at most `limit`. Consequently, renderFeed's call with 20 iterates over all input entries and extends its initially 20-slot output array beyond 20 entries.

findings.title: Restore the requested limit
findings.whyItBreaks: For every positive limit, recentEntries now returns every entry rather than at most limit entries. renderFeed calls it with 20, then copies the entire returned page, expanding its result beyond 20 entries.

findings.title: Restore the limit slice for positive limits
findings.whyItBreaks: For any positive limit smaller than all.length, recentEntries now returns every reversed entry rather than at most limit. renderFeed passes 20 at line 9; with more than 20 entries, its assignment loop extends the 20-slot output array and renders all entries.

findings.title: Count only emitted manifest entries
findings.whyItBreaks: When any entry is stale, rows contains only live entries while the unchanged header call uses entries.length. The generated # entry-count therefore claims more rows than the manifest contains, breaking consumers that use the header to validate or preallocate for the emitted records.

findings.title: Count only emitted manifest entries
findings.whyItBreaks: For any stale entry, the new filter removes its data row but line 22 still passes entries.length to the # entry-count header. A manifest with one live and one stale entry therefore declares entry-count: 2 while containing one entry, breaking consumers that use the header to validate or read the manifest.

findings.title: Count only emitted manifest entries
findings.whyItBreaks: When any input has stale=true, its row is removed but the unchanged '# entry-count' header still uses entries.length. Consumers parsing the manifest receive a declared count larger than the number of rows, violating the manifest's count contract.

findings.title: Preserve the exported FormatLegacyID compatibility API
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing consumers that call ids.FormatLegacyID will no longer compile after upgrading. The deleted function produced a distinct legacy identifier format, so this is an observable public-contract removal rather than an internal cleanup.

findings.title: Retain FormatLegacyID as a compatibility wrapper
findings.whyItBreaks: FormatLegacyID is an exported package API. Removing it makes any existing consumer that formats persisted or interoperable legacy IDs fail to compile on upgrade, with no replacement or deprecation path.

findings.title: Restore the removed shippingQuote export
findings.whyItBreaks: shippingQuote was an exported API from this module and is now absent. Existing consumers importing it from src/orders will fail to compile or load after upgrading, despite the equivalent implementation existing as quoteShipping.

findings.title: Preserve the shippingQuote public export
findings.whyItBreaks: shippingQuote was an exported API from this module but is removed. Existing consumers importing it from src/orders will fail type-checking or module loading after upgrading, even though the equivalent calculation now exists under a different name.

findings.title: Restore execute's string result
findings.whyItBreaks: execute is exported with a string return contract, but every invocation now throws before returning a value. The prior implementation transformed and returned the input, so existing consumers will receive an exception instead of the expected uppercase string.

findings.title: Restore execute's string result
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported execute(input: string): string API previously returned input.toUpperCase(), but now unconditionally throws. Every consumer calling this public function receives an exception instead of the promised result.

findings.title: Restore execute’s string result
findings.whyItBreaks: Every call to execute now throws "always fails", so no caller can receive the uppercase string that the base implementation returned.

findings.title: Do not reject viewers before the read-only branch
findings.whyItBreaks: An active viewer with fewer than five attempts now makes isEligible return false, so handle returns "rejected" at line 24. The existing viewer branch at line 25, which previously returned "read-only", is therefore unreachable.

findings.title: Preserve the viewer read-only path
findings.whyItBreaks: An active viewer below the attempt limit previously passed isEligible and returned "read-only" from handle. The added role check now returns false first, so handle returns "rejected" and its viewer branch at line 25 is unreachable.

findings.title: Preserve the viewer read-only path
findings.whyItBreaks: An active viewer below the attempt limit previously reached handle()'s "read-only" result, but is now rejected by isEligible() first. This makes the existing viewer-specific behavior unreachable.

findings.title: Keep unpaid orders saveable as drafts
findings.whyItBreaks: The new shared payment condition makes `saveDraft({ state: "draft", payment: "missing" })` return "blocked". Saving a draft is distinct from submitting an order and should remain possible before payment.

findings.title: Keep saving drafts independent of payment
findings.whyItBreaks: For `{ state: "draft", payment: "missing" }`, this now returns false, so `saveDraft` returns "blocked" instead of "saved". Payment can legitimately govern submission, but it must not prevent persisting an unpaid draft.

findings.title: Do not require payment to save drafts
findings.whyItBreaks: `saveDraft` shares `canProceed`; consequently a normal draft with `payment: "missing"` now returns `"blocked"` instead of `"saved"`. Payment can govern order submission, but it should not prevent persisting a draft.

findings.title: Read files from the snapshot commit
findings.whyItBreaks: The snapshot's commit is the requested channel head, but files are always read from stable. For any channel whose head differs from stable, consumers receive a self-inconsistent snapshot: commit/channel identify one revision while files describe another.

findings.title: Read snapshot files from the advertised commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any channel whose head differs from stable, the returned Snapshot.commit and Snapshot.channel describe that channel, while Snapshot.files is taken from stable. Consumers can therefore publish or inspect a mismatched file set.

findings.title: Read snapshot files from the reported commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any channel other than stable, the returned Snapshot.commit identifies that channel’s head while Snapshot.files describes stable. Consumers cannot reliably read the files for the reported commit.

findings.title: Honor the limit parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: Calling build(prefix, limit=2) still returns 10 entries because the loop uses the hard-coded max_count = 10. The new public parameter promises caller-controlled output limiting but has no observable effect.

findings.title: Honor the supplied limit
findings.whyItBreaks: `build(prefix, limit=3)` still returns 10 entries because the loop uses the unchanged hard-coded `max_count = 10`. The new public parameter promises an observable output cap but has no effect.

findings.title: Honor the requested limit
findings.whyItBreaks: The public build(prefix, limit=10) signature promises a caller-controlled limit, but max_count remains hard-coded to 10. For example, build("item", 3) still returns 10 entries.

findings.title: Reject non-positive values in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: `parse_positive_int(-1)` and `parse_positive_int(0)` return successfully, despite the public name promising positive integers; `charge` consequently produces -100 or 0 cents.

findings.title: Reject non-positive values in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: Despite its public name, parse_positive_int(0) returns 0 and parse_positive_int(-1) returns -1. charge consequently produces zero or negative cents instead of rejecting values outside the promised positive domain.

findings.title: Validate the positivity promised by parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: `parse_positive_int(-1)` returns `-1` and `parse_positive_int(0)` returns `0`, despite its public name promising a positive integer. `charge` therefore produces negative or zero charges.

findings.title: Preserve the caller's DataFrame
findings.whyItBreaks: The prior implementation applied mappings to df.copy() and returned the independent result. This change writes directly to df and returns the same object, so callers that retain df for later use silently observe their original data overwritten.

findings.title: Preserve the caller DataFrame when applying mappings
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation copied df before assignment; this version writes directly through df.loc and returns that same object. Callers that retain df for later use now observe mapped values unexpectedly, rather than receiving an independently transformed result.

findings.title: Preserve the caller DataFrame
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously the function applied mapping changes to df.copy() and returned the new frame. The changed assignment writes directly into df, so callers that retain df for later use now observe unexpected value changes.

findings.title: Validate positivity before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: `parse_positive_int("-5")` returns -5 and `parse_positive_int("0")` returns 0, contradicting its public positive-value contract; `charge("-5")` consequently returns -500.

findings.title: Validate that parsed integers are positive
findings.whyItBreaks: `parse_positive_int` is public and promises a positive result, but its body accepts `0` and negative inputs unchanged (for example, `"-3"` returns `-3`). Callers can therefore receive values that violate the advertised contract; `charge("-3")` produces `-300`.

findings.title: Reject non-positive inputs
findings.whyItBreaks: `parse_positive_int("-3")` returns `-3`, contradicting its public name; `charge("-3")` consequently returns `-300` rather than rejecting or defaulting the invalid amount.

findings.title: Borrow items when logging them
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!(items)` evaluates and returns its argument by value; as a standalone expression it consumes the `Vec<String>`. The subsequent `items.len()` borrows a moved value, producing Rust error E0382 and preventing the crate from compiling.

findings.title: Compute paths from the advertised base revision
findings.whyItBreaks: `fromRevision` remains the revision resolved from `pinnedTag`, while `changedPaths` is computed from `latest`. Consumers replay these paths on `fromRevision` per the public `Changeset` contract, so they can apply a path set from an unrelated revision.

findings.title: Compute paths from the advertised revision
findings.whyItBreaks: The Changeset contract says consumers replay changedPaths on fromRevision, but this now reads paths from latest while returning the pinned revision as fromRevision. When the revisions differ, consumers receive a changeset that does not apply to its advertised base.

findings.title: Compute paths from the advertised revision
findings.whyItBreaks: The public Changeset contract says changedPaths are computed against fromRevision for replay. This now resolves paths from "latest" while returning the pinned revision as fromRevision, so consumers replaying onto fromRevision can apply a path set from the wrong baseline.

findings.title: Update queries to use the renamed email column
findings.whyItBreaks: After this migration, users.email no longer exists, but src/query.sql still executes `SELECT email FROM users`; that query fails instead of returning user contact data.

findings.title: Update the query for the renamed column
findings.whyItBreaks: After this migration, `users.email` no longer exists, but `src/query.sql:1` still executes `SELECT email FROM users`. Any deployment that applies the migration will cause that query to fail with a missing-column error.

findings.title: Update queries for the renamed email column
findings.whyItBreaks: After this migration, the users.email column no longer exists, but src/query.sql still executes SELECT email FROM users. Any consumer of that query will fail with a missing-column database error.

findings.title: Remove and rotate the committed live billing key
findings.whyItBreaks: The literal `bk_live_...` production credential is exposed in repository history and every build artifact, allowing anyone with repository access to authenticate as the billing client. Replacing the environment lookup also prevents safe per-environment credential configuration.

findings.title: Restore the environment-provided billing credential
findings.whyItBreaks: Every consumer of exported makeClient() now receives the committed bk_live credential, regardless of its deployment's BILLING_API_KEY. This exposes a production-shaped secret in version control, prevents per-environment credential selection/rotation, and turns a missing configuration error into use of a shared credential.

findings.title: Restore environment-sourced billing credentials
findings.whyItBreaks: This commits a `bk_live_` billing API key into source control and causes every deployment to use that shared live credential, regardless of its configured secret. Repository readers and build logs can obtain the key, and normal environment-level rotation or isolation no longer works.

findings.title: Restore the missing-settings fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings returns None when path does not exist (app/config.py:6-7). startup then indexes None at the changed return path, raising TypeError rather than starting with one worker as it did before this change.

findings.title: Restore defaults when the settings file is absent
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings returns None when path does not exist (app/config.py:6-7). After removing the None fallback, startup evaluates settings["workers"] on None and raises TypeError instead of starting with the previous default worker configuration.

findings.title: Restore defaults when the settings file is absent
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings returns None when path does not exist (app/config.py:6-7). This changed return statement then evaluates settings["workers"] on None and raises TypeError, whereas the base revision returned the default worker count of 1.

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit fails, Charge logs the error and returns nil at line 19. This exported API now conflates a declined/failed charge with a successful one, so callers cannot stop fulfillment, retry, or notify the user.

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit returns an error, Charge only logs it and returns nil. Its exported error-returning API now conflates a declined/failed charge with a successful charge, so external callers can proceed as though payment completed.

findings.title: Return gateway failures from Charge
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit fails, Charge only logs the error and returns nil. Callers therefore treat declined or failed charges as successful and can continue with fulfillment or persistence.

findings.title: Include tenant ID in the settings cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: cacheKey("theme") is identical for every tenant. After settingsFor("tenant-a", "theme", store) caches tenant A's value, settingsFor("tenant-b", "theme", store) hits that entry at line 13 and returns tenant A's setting without calling store.fetch for tenant B. The paired invalidate signature change also prevents callers using the former invalidate(tenantId, name) API from deleting the corresponding entry.

findings.title: Include the tenant in the cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: settingsFor still fetches values using tenantId, but all tenants now share `settings:${name}`. After tenant A caches a setting, tenant B requesting the same name receives tenant A's value without calling its store.

findings.title: Preserve tenant-scoped invalidation compatibility
findings.whyItBreaks: This exported function previously accepted `(tenantId, name)`. Existing TypeScript consumers no longer typecheck; JavaScript consumers that retain the old call pass tenantId as `name`, so the intended setting entry is not invalidated.

findings.title: Include tenant ID in the settings cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: settingsFor still fetches values per tenant (store.fetch(tenantId, name)), but all tenants now share the cache entry `settings:<name>`. After tenant A reads a setting, tenant B requesting the same name receives tenant A's cached value without calling its own store. The matching global invalidation can also evict another tenant's entry.

findings.title: Serialize reservations before awaiting persistence
findings.whyItBreaks: With stock=1, two concurrent reserve calls both read remaining=1 before either await resumes. Both save 0, both return true, and only one unit is recorded as removed, so the system confirms two reservations for one item.

findings.title: Preserve the synchronous reserve API or ship a migration
findings.whyItBreaks: reserve previously returned a boolean but now returns Promise<boolean>. Existing JavaScript callers such as `if (inventory.reserve(sku))` treat Promise<false> as truthy and proceed with an unavailable reservation; typed callers expecting boolean also stop compiling.

findings.title: Keep the Inventory constructor backward compatible
findings.whyItBreaks: Inventory was publicly constructible with no arguments. Requiring a Store makes every existing `new Inventory()` call fail at compile time or construct an object without the required dependency at runtime.

findings.title: Serialize reservations for each SKU
findings.whyItBreaks: The await yields after reading stock but before updating it. With stock=1, two concurrent reserve calls both read 1, both save 0, both return true, and only one unit is deducted. This permits overselling.

findings.title: Serialize concurrent reservations for the same SKU
findings.whyItBreaks: With stock=1, two concurrent reserve calls both read remaining=1 before either await completes. Both save 0, both set local stock to 0, and both return true, so two reservations succeed for one unit.

findings.title: Preserve retry’s millisecond backoff contract
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff(0) now returns 1,000 milliseconds, but retry still calls sleep(backoff(a) * 1000). After its first failed attempt, retry waits 1,000,000 ms (about 16.7 minutes) instead of 1 second; later retries are similarly inflated.

findings.title: Keep retry delays in milliseconds
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() now returns milliseconds, and schedulePoll was updated accordingly. retry() still multiplies its result by 1000 before passing it to its millisecond sleep helper, so its first retry waits 1,000,000 ms (about 16.7 minutes) instead of 1,000 ms.

findings.title: Keep retry delays in milliseconds
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff(0) now returns 1000 (milliseconds), but retry still calls sleep(backoff(a) * 1000) at src/jobs/retry.ts:12. The first retry therefore waits 1,000,000 ms (16m40s) instead of 1 second; capped retries wait 30,000,000 ms (over 8 hours).

findings.title: Propagate the file close error
findings.whyItBreaks: The deferred f.Close() return value is ignored. Previously Save returned f.Close() after a successful flush, so a close-time write/persistence failure was visible to callers. Save is exported, and this change makes such failures indistinguishable from a successful save.

findings.title: Propagate the file-close error
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous successful path returned f.Close()'s error, but the deferred Close result is discarded. A delayed filesystem error during close is therefore reported as a successful Save, leaving callers unable to distinguish a fully persisted file from a failed save.

findings.title: Propagate the file-close error
findings.whyItBreaks: The deferred f.Close() return value is discarded. If Flush succeeds but Close fails, Save returns nil even though the prior implementation returned that failure to its caller.

findings.title: Include the page endpoint when collecting rows
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns a half-open [start, end) interval, but range(start, end - 1) excludes its final valid index. Consequently render_page and summarize silently omit the last row of each non-empty page; a one-row page renders empty.

findings.title: Include the end row in page windows
findings.whyItBreaks: The half-open bounds helper returns end as the exclusive boundary, but range(start, end - 1) stops one position early. A page of size 1 becomes empty, and every larger page omits its last row; render_page and summarize therefore silently lose rows.

findings.title: Include the page endpoint when collecting rows
findings.whyItBreaks: The half-open bounds helper returns end as the exclusive page boundary, but range(start, end - 1) excludes the row at end - 1. Thus a one-row page renders empty and every other page loses its final row; summarize consequently drops one row per page.

findings.title: Return entries before their TTL expires
findings.whyItBreaks: A newly stored entry has an age near zero, which is not greater than ttlMs, so get() immediately deletes it and returns null. Conversely, entries older than the TTL are returned indefinitely.

findings.title: Remove every consecutive completed job
findings.whyItBreaks: Splicing during forEach shifts the next job into the current index, then forEach advances past it. For [{id:"a",done:true},{id:"b",done:true}], job b remains in the returned queue.

findings.title: Restore fresh-entry cache hits
findings.whyItBreaks: A newly stored entry has age near zero, so it fails `age > ttlMs`, is deleted, and returns null. Conversely, entries older than the TTL are returned as valid cache hits.

findings.title: Do not skip consecutive completed jobs
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing an element during forward `forEach` shifts the next job into the current index, then `forEach` advances past it. For example, `[done, done, pending]` returns `[done, pending]`.

findings.title: Preserve the caller's input array
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation returned a filtered copy. This version splices `jobs` and returns the same object, so callers retaining the input array now lose completed jobs as a side effect.

findings.title: Return entries only while they are unexpired
findings.whyItBreaks: A newly stored entry has age near zero, so `age > ttlMs` is false and `get` deletes it and returns null. Conversely, expired entries are returned indefinitely.

findings.title: Filter completed jobs without skipping adjacent entries
findings.whyItBreaks: Splicing during `forEach` shifts the next job into the current index, then `forEach` advances past it. For `[done, done]`, the second completed job remains in the returned queue; this also changes the prior non-mutating API behavior.

findings.title: Preserve the zero result for an empty input
findings.whyItBreaks: With rows=[], reduce produces 0 and division by rows.length produces NaN. The prior public behavior returned 0, so consumers that persist, display, or calculate with an empty aggregate now receive an invalid numeric value.

findings.title: Avoid sorting the caller's array in place
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort mutates rows. Callers that reuse their input after calling busiest now observe it reordered by amount, whereas the previous implementation sorted a defensive copy.

findings.title: Preserve the empty-input average
findings.whyItBreaks: For an empty rows array, reduce produces 0 and dividing by rows.length (0) returns NaN instead of the previous 0. Callers receiving a numeric average can no longer use the result in arithmetic or display it reliably.

findings.title: Do not reorder the caller's rows
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort mutates rows in place. The previous implementation copied before sorting, so callers that invoke busiest(rows) and subsequently use rows now observe an unexpected descending reorder.

findings.title: Preserve the empty-input result for averageAmount
findings.whyItBreaks: For an empty array, total is 0 and rows.length is 0, so this now returns NaN instead of the previously established 0 result.

findings.title: Avoid sorting the caller's rows array in place
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort mutates rows. Callers that reuse their input now observe it reordered, whereas the prior implementation explicitly sorted a copy.

findings.title: Restore numeric score ordering
findings.whyItBreaks: Array#sort() without a comparator orders numbers as strings. For players ordered as scores [2, 11, 10] with n=1, rankScores returns [2, 11, 10], so cutoff is 2 and topPlayers returns the first input player (score 2) instead of the score-11 player.

findings.title: Sort scores numerically before reversing
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort() without a comparator orders numbers as strings. For scores [2, 10, 1], rankScores returns [2, 10, 1], so topPlayers(players, 1) uses cutoff 2 and can return the score-2 player instead of the score-10 player.

findings.title: Restore numeric descending score sorting
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() compares numbers as strings. For scores [2, 10], it produces [10, 2] and reverse() yields [2, 10], so topPlayers(..., 1) derives a cutoff of 2 and can return the 2-point player instead of the 10-point player.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Using == can stop at the first differing character, exposing prefix-match timing information for the HMAC. The previous hmac.compare_digest call avoided this side channel before handle() authorized processor execution.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Using `==` exposes comparison timing differences for attacker-controlled signatures. Repeated requests can use those differences to recover a valid HMAC and reach the authenticated webhook-processing path.

findings.title: Use constant-time comparison for webhook signatures
findings.whyItBreaks: Normal string equality can reveal how much of the expected HMAC matches through response timing. An attacker able to measure repeated webhook responses can use that oracle to incrementally forge a valid signature and reach processor(payload).

findings.title: Keep balance updates in the ledger transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The ledger insert commits when the `with db.transaction()` block exits at line 23. If either subsequent account update fails, `transfer` raises after a durable ledger entry has been recorded but before both balances are updated. Previously all three writes rolled back together.

findings.title: Keep ledger and balance updates in one transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction commits the ledger insert at line 23 before either balance update runs. If either update fails, the ledger entry remains committed; additionally, failure of the credit update can leave a committed debit without its matching credit.

findings.title: Keep ledger and balance updates in one transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction exits immediately after `_record_ledger`, committing the ledger row before either balance update runs. If either `_apply_balances` statement raises (for example, a database error or a failed constraint), the transfer is recorded as completed while one or both account balances remain unchanged; the prior implementation rolled all three writes back together.

findings.title: Keep billing-day calculation in UTC
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation deliberately used UTC for every date component. This change uses the process-local timezone, so the same instant can produce different billing keys by deployment region; for example, 2026-01-01T00:30:00Z becomes 2025-12-31 on a host in America/Los_Angeles. That changes sameBillingDay classification and can assign usage to the wrong billing date.

findings.title: Preserve UTC when deriving the billing day
findings.whyItBreaks: The prior implementation explicitly used UTC accessors. This now uses the process host timezone, so the same instant can receive a different billing day: for example, 2026-01-01T00:30:00Z is returned as 2025-12-31 when the host runs in America/Los_Angeles, rather than 2026-01-01.

findings.title: Keep billing-day formatting in UTC
findings.whyItBreaks: The prior implementation deliberately used all three UTC accessors. This now formats the runtime host's local calendar date instead: for `2026-08-30T16:30:00.000Z`, a UTC+08 host returns `2026-08-31` while the previous and timezone-independent billing day is `2026-08-30`. Billing-day keys and `sameBillingDay` results therefore vary by deployment timezone and change at local rather than UTC midnight.

findings.title: Restore tenant scoping in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: After tenant A reads account `alice`, a request for tenant B and account `alice` finds the same `memo` entry and returns tenant A's Profile without calling fetchProfile. The Profile contract includes `tenant`, making the wrong-tenant result observable.

findings.title: Restore tenant isolation in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: Two tenants using the same account value now share one memo entry. After tenant A's profile is cached, readProfile("tenant-b", sameAccount, ...) returns tenant A's Profile at line 16 without calling fetchProfile, leaking tenant-scoped data across the isolation boundary.

findings.title: Keep tenant in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: After `readProfile('tenant-a', 'shared-account', fetchProfile)` caches a profile, `readProfile('tenant-b', 'shared-account', fetchProfile)` uses the same `shared-account` key and returns tenant-a’s cached Profile without calling the tenant-b fetcher. This leaks/cross-contaminates tenant-scoped profile data.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key failures from load
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key previously threw `Error("missing: <key>")`; it now returns `""`, which is indistinguishable from a stored empty-string value. `loadAll` consequently returns a partial-looking successful result instead of propagating the missing-key failure.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors from load
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key previously threw; it now returns "", which is indistinguishable from a stored empty string. loadAll consequently returns a plausible string array for incomplete input instead of reporting the missing key.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key now returns "", which is indistinguishable from a key intentionally stored with an empty value. loadAll therefore returns a seemingly successful result containing "" where it previously propagated the missing-key error, so callers cannot reject incomplete input.

findings.title: Make retryBackground non-blocking or rename it
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported name promises background execution, but the implementation invokes fn synchronously before returning. A blocking fn therefore blocks the caller, contrary to the API contract.

findings.title: Expose retryBackground exhaustion to callers
findings.whyItBreaks: Every exception is discarded and exhaustion falls through as void, exactly like success. This new exported API forces callers to treat a failed background operation as successful.

findings.title: Preserve the existing Config timeoutMs contract
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing TypeScript consumers passing the formerly valid `{ maxAttempts, timeoutMs }` config no longer compile because `timeout` and unrelated `retries` are required. JavaScript consumers still run, but `config.timeout` is undefined, making `deadline` NaN; `Date.now() > deadline` is always false, so retry() no longer enforces its timeout.

findings.title: Propagate exhausted background retry failures
findings.whyItBreaks: retryBackground catches every callback error and ultimately returns void whether the callback succeeded or every attempt failed. As an exported API, this forces callers to treat a failed operation as successful completion and gives them no error or result signal on which to avoid follow-on work.

findings.title: Preserve the existing Config contract
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing TypeScript callers supplying the exported `{ maxAttempts, timeoutMs }` shape now fail to compile because `timeout` and `retries` are required. Existing JavaScript callers have `config.timeout === undefined`, making `Date.now() + config.timeout` NaN; `Date.now() > deadline` is then always false, so the timeout no longer limits retries.

findings.title: Schedule retryBackground work asynchronously
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported name promises background behavior, but the implementation calls `fn()` and performs every retry synchronously before returning. A caller relying on this API not to block its current request or UI path instead blocks for all callback execution time.

findings.title: Surface retryBackground exhaustion
findings.whyItBreaks: Every callback exception is discarded and the exported function returns void after the final failed attempt. Callers cannot distinguish a successful retry from total failure, so they can continue as if background work completed.

findings.title: Handle numeric values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: `FieldProps` now accepts `number`, but numbers have no `length`. TypeScript rejects this access on `string | number`; if emitted without type-checking, `<Field value={42}>` renders `len=undefined` rather than a meaningful value.

findings.title: Handle numeric Field values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed public prop type permits numbers, but numbers have no `length` property. TypeScript rejects this expression; if emitted JavaScript runs, `<Field value={42}>` renders `len=undefined` instead of a meaningful label.

findings.title: Handle numeric values before reading `.length`
findings.whyItBreaks: `FieldProps.value` now permits `number`, but numbers do not have a `length` property. TypeScript rejects this expression, blocking the application build.

findings.title: Remove the credential from workflow output
findings.whyItBreaks: Expanding $TOKEN in echo sends the deployment secret to the runner log stream. This creates a credential disclosure path and relies on log masking remaining complete for every secret representation.

findings.title: Preserve the Git output buffer limit
findings.whyItBreaks: `git diff` at line 140 is captured through this wrapper. Removing `maxBuffer: 64 MiB` restores Node's 1 MiB default, so a PR whose patch exceeds that size terminates the child process with a max-buffer error and the review reports failure instead of reviewing the PR.

findings.title: Retain a buffer large enough for Git diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync defaults maxBuffer to 1 MiB. This helper captures the complete output of `git diff` at line 140, so a PR with a diff larger than 1 MiB now terminates with ENOBUFS and the review fails instead of posting results. The previous 64 MiB limit handled these valid PRs.

findings.title: Restore a buffer large enough for review patches
findings.whyItBreaks: `git()` captures `git diff` output at line 140. Removing its explicit 64 MiB `maxBuffer` restores Node's 1 MiB default; PRs with diffs larger than that are terminated with a max-buffer error, so the action throws before submitting any review or check result.

findings.title: Restore the read-only sandbox for review runs
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `-s read-only` makes the spawned `codex exec` run with its default write-capable sandbox in `opts.repoPath`. `runCodex` accepts an arbitrary prompt, does not snapshot or verify the worktree, and returns only the model output, so a review invocation can now alter source files or create artifacts while being presented as a read-only review.

findings.title: Restore read-only sandboxing for review runs
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `-s read-only` runs the Codex subprocess with its default sandbox rather than the explicit non-mutating mode. A review prompt or repository-provided instruction can therefore cause writes in `opts.repoPath`, corrupting the checkout/PR state that Needlefish is supposed to inspect only.

findings.title: Keep the review subprocess read-only
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `-s read-only` delegates the sandbox policy to the Codex configuration/default. The subprocess runs with `cwd: opts.repoPath`, so a prompt-injected or mistaken model action can now create, modify, or delete files in the repository being reviewed. This breaks the review runner's non-mutating isolation guarantee.

findings.title: Diff the configured PR head, not the checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_HEAD_SHA names the PR tip but HEAD is a different checkout revision (such as an Actions pull-request merge checkout), the patch and changed-file list are computed for HEAD while the resulting review/check is posted to headSha. The reviewer can therefore report findings for a different commit than the PR commit it annotates; using baseSha directly also includes base-branch-only changes when baseSha is ahead of the PR's merge base.

findings.title: Diff against the PR head SHA instead of checkout HEAD
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_HEAD_SHA is supplied and the Actions checkout is a different commit (for example, GitHub's synthetic merge commit), the bundle's headSha and the patch/changedFiles describe different revisions. Needlefish can review merge-only/base changes, omit PR-tip changes, and attach results to the PR head commit despite having analyzed HEAD.

findings.title: Diff from the merge base to the selected PR head
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_BASE_SHA is the current base tip after it has advanced beyond the branch point, `git diff baseSha HEAD` includes base-only changes in the review. It also ignores the already-selected `headSha` when PR_HEAD_SHA differs from the local checkout's HEAD, so the bundle can claim one head SHA while reviewing another commit.

findings.title: Preserve literal prompt payloads during replacement
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace interprets $&, $`, $', and $$ in a string replacement. Bundle.patch is raw PR text, and candidate findings are model-produced text, so a legitimate dollar sequence can be expanded instead of retained. For example, $& in a patch becomes {{PATCH}} or {{BUNDLE}}, while $' injects the remainder of the template into the embedded payload. This corrupts the review/critic prompt and can cause the reviewer to inspect different content from the actual diff.

findings.title: Preserve literal dollar sequences in the patch prompt
findings.whyItBreaks: `String.prototype.replace` interprets `$&`, `$`` and `$'` in a replacement string. A reviewed patch containing a literal `$&` is rendered as `{{PATCH}}` rather than the original code, so the critic receives a corrupted diff and can miss or misattribute findings.

findings.title: Preserve literal dollar sequences when inserting the patch
findings.whyItBreaks: String.replace interprets $&, $`, $', and $$ in a string replacement. A PR patch containing $& is inserted into the critic prompt as {{PATCH}} rather than the literal source text; other sequences can inject surrounding prompt text. The critic therefore reviews a corrupted diff.

findings.title: Keep fallback reviews bound to the analyzed commit
findings.whyItBreaks: The review result is computed from the captured headSha, but when the initial review POST fails this fallback now omits commit_id. GitHub then targets the PR's most recent commit. If a push arrives between analysis and the retry, a stale REQUEST_CHANGES verdict is attached to the newer commit, potentially blocking changes that fixed the finding; the corresponding check run remains attached to the original headSha.

findings.title: Keep the reviewed commit when retrying the review request
findings.whyItBreaks: The review content is computed from headSha, but this fallback now omits commit_id. GitHub then defaults the review to the PR's most recent commit. If a new commit is pushed while review() is running and the initial request fails (for example due to invalid inline comments), the fallback posts a review of the old diff as though it reviewed the new tip.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of fabricating defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: A malformed finding such as `{}` now becomes a P1 bug at an empty file and line 0, with empty rationale/fix, instead of propagating a malformed-output error. Callers of either exported normalizer cannot distinguish invalid model output from a real finding and may report or persist the fabricated finding.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of manufacturing valid ones
findings.whyItBreaks: Inputs previously rejected for invalid severity/category, missing file/text fields, or non-positive line numbers now become a Finding with defaults such as severity P1, file "", and lineStart 0. This exported API therefore makes an invalid review indistinguishable from a real finding, so consumers can act on unusable locations and fallback metadata.

findings.title: Preserve the strict normalization option
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the exported strict parameter is a source-breaking API change: existing TypeScript callers using normalizeReview(raw, false) no longer compile. Its former documented-by-behavior mode also dropped malformed findings; the replacement instead manufactures fallback findings.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of fabricating defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid review output no longer remains distinguishable from a valid finding. For example, `{}` now becomes a P1 "Untitled finding" with `file: ""` and line `0`, while invalid coordinates such as `-1` or `"x"` are returned as `-1` or `NaN`. `normalizeReview` therefore accepts malformed model output and can present or act on fabricated findings rather than rejecting it (or omitting it in the former non-strict mode).

findings.title: Restore explicit repository selection for manual PR lookup
findings.whyItBreaks: workflow_dispatch has no pull_request head/base values, so it takes this branch before the checkout at line 42. `gh pr view` resolves an omitted repository only from a local repository or `GH_REPO`; removing `-R "$REPO"` leaves neither available in a fresh runner workspace. The manual workflow therefore fails resolving refs (or may use stale self-hosted workspace repository context) instead of reviewing the selected PR.

findings.title: Keep explicit repository selection for manual PR resolution
findings.whyItBreaks: The workflow_dispatch path reaches these commands before any actions/checkout step. Without -R "$REPO" (or GH_REPO), gh pr view must infer a repository from the runner's current Git checkout. A clean self-hosted workspace has no such checkout, so gh fails to resolve the PR. Because the failing command is embedded in echo command substitution, the step still writes empty head/base outputs; checkout then proceeds without the requested PR ref.

findings.title: Keep the explicit repository when resolving manual PR refs
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, this is the first step and no checkout has occurred yet. Removing -R leaves gh pr view without a repository context, so it cannot reliably resolve PR_NUM; on a clean runner it fails rather than producing head/base SHAs, and on a reused self-hosted workspace it may use a stale repository.

findings.title: Reject malformed review output instead of defaulting it
findings.whyItBreaks: Inputs such as null, or an object missing findings/checked/residual_risks, previously raised a malformed-output error but now produce an empty summary and empty arrays. This exported normalizer therefore makes an invalid reviewer response indistinguishable from a legitimate review with no findings or blocking risks, allowing downstream consumers to act on failed or truncated output.

findings.title: Preserve malformed review-output errors
findings.whyItBreaks: Inputs missing required fields (including a non-object response, missing summary, or non-array checked/findings/residual_risks) previously threw a malformed-review error. They now return an empty/partial RawReview, so callers cannot distinguish an invalid agent response from a legitimate zero-finding review and may report it as a successful clean review.

findings.title: Preserve malformed-review errors
findings.whyItBreaks: Inputs such as null, {}, or a response missing findings now return a valid RawReview with an empty summary and no findings instead of rejecting malformed upstream output. This exported API forces callers to conflate an LLM/parser failure with a legitimate clean review.

findings.title: Resolve PR refs for manual dispatch before checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, github.event.pull_request is absent. The expression at line 29 therefore falls back to github.ref (the branch selected when dispatching the workflow), not the head SHA of inputs.pr_number. Lines 45-46 likewise pass empty PR_BASE_SHA and PR_HEAD_SHA. A manually requested review can thus install and run the tool from an unrelated branch instead of the requested PR; the previous Resolve PR refs step explicitly queried the requested PR to avoid this.

findings.title: Restore selected PR ref resolution for manual runs
findings.whyItBreaks: A workflow_dispatch payload has no pull_request object. These expressions therefore select the dispatch branch for checkout, default BASE_REF to main, and pass empty PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA. This repository's origin default branch is master, so the new fetch requests nonexistent refs/heads/main and aborts before the review. Even where main exists, a manual run can review the dispatch branch rather than the PR selected by pr_number.

findings.title: Resolve the selected PR refs for manual dispatch
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, github.event.pull_request is absent. The checkout expression therefore falls back to github.ref (the workflow's default-branch ref), while PR_BASE_SHA and PR_HEAD_SHA resolve to empty strings. A manually requested PR review consequently does not use the requested PR head/base; before this change, the Resolve PR refs step queried those exact values using the supplied pr_number.

findings.title: Restore the buffer required to capture large diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: `runLocal` captures the entire `git diff` output at line 100. Without `maxBuffer`, `spawnSync` uses Node’s 1 MiB default, so a larger legitimate PR aborts before review instead of producing a bundle.

findings.title: Retain capacity for large git diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: `runLocal` obtains the entire patch through `git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"])` at line 100. Without `maxBuffer`, Node's `spawnSync` default is 1 MiB, so a legitimate review diff exceeding that size fails with `ENOBUFS` instead of producing a review. The previous implementation explicitly supported up to 64 MiB.

findings.title: Restore a buffer large enough for Git diff output
findings.whyItBreaks: `runLocal` reads the complete `git diff` output at line 100. Without `maxBuffer`, `spawnSync` uses Node's 1 MiB default, so a valid review with a diff exceeding that size fails before reaching `review()`; the previous 64 MiB limit supported those inputs.

findings.title: Keep failed reviews failing
findings.whyItBreaks: When review() throws, the posted Needlefish check now concludes neutral despite the message stating the review did not pass. GitHub treats neutral as a successful required-status conclusion, so a repository requiring this posted Needlefish check can permit merging although the review never ran successfully.

findings.title: Keep review errors failing
findings.whyItBreaks: When review() throws, this path explicitly says the PR did not pass, but posts its Needlefish check with conclusion "neutral" instead of "failure". GitHub treats neutral checks as non-failing, so branch protection requiring this check can permit merging despite no completed review.

findings.title: Keep failed reviews as failed checks
findings.whyItBreaks: When review execution throws, this downgrades the posted Needlefish check from failure to neutral even though its summary says the review did not pass. Consumers of the Needlefish check can no longer treat its conclusion as a failure signal.

findings.title: Keep the reviewer implementation on a trusted checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: A same-repository PR can modify src/cli.ts, then this job executes that modified code with GH_TOKEN and pull-request/check write permissions. The PR can suppress or forge its own review result, defeating the review trust boundary; it also runs arbitrary PR code on the self-hosted runner.

findings.title: Restore a checkout that contains the reviewer package
findings.whyItBreaks: The reviewed head tree contains only .github/workflows/review.yml and .needlefish/answers.json; it has no package.json, pnpm-lock.yaml, src/cli.ts, or node_modules/.bin/tsx. Installing at the PR checkout cannot provide tsx, and the review step therefore cannot execute.

The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.

findings.title: Keep a checkout of the Needlefish tool
findings.whyItBreaks: At d515d1a this repository contains only .github/workflows/review.yml and .needlefish/answers.json: it has neither package.json nor src/cli.ts. The new root-level `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` therefore cannot install dependencies, and the subsequent `tsx src/cli.ts` path cannot exist. PR review workflows will fail without producing a review.

facts.meaning: The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.
The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.

findings.title: Restore the trusted reviewer checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The job checks out the PR head at lines 43-47, installs its dependency graph at line 51, then executes its src/cli.ts here. A same-repository PR can therefore alter the CLI or package lifecycle behavior and run it on the self-hosted runner while GH_TOKEN is available (line 56) with pull-request and check write permissions. The removed separate main checkout was the boundary preventing a reviewed PR from controlling the reviewer.

facts.meaning: The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.
The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.

findings.title: Preserve canonicalization of severity input
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, `{ severity: " p1 " }` and `{ severity: "p1" }` normalized to `P1`; the changed exact-membership check rejects both and returns `P3`. This regresses the exported normalizer's handling of raw review JSON and misclassifies findings as low priority.

findings.title: Normalize severity before validating it
findings.whyItBreaks: A finding with severity " p1 " or "p1" previously normalized to "P1" but now fails the exact enum check and is silently returned as "P3". normalizeReview passes untyped parsed finding data through this function, so compatible review payloads are downgraded.

findings.title: Keep GitHub credentials out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the explicit sanitized environment makes spawnSync inherit GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN. The invoked Codex process can inspect the repository and consume untrusted review input; granting it ambient GitHub credentials permits repository instructions, dependencies, or invoked tooling to use or exfiltrate credentials despite this wrapper's read-only sandbox argument.

findings.title: Keep GitHub tokens out of the Codex child environment
findings.whyItBreaks: Without an explicit env object, spawnSync inherits process.env, so GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN are now available to the Codex subprocess. This wrapper executes an agent against a supplied repository/prompt; injected instructions or subprocess commands can read and exfiltrate those credentials despite the read-only filesystem sandbox.

findings.title: Keep GitHub credentials out of the Codex child
findings.whyItBreaks: Without an explicit env object, spawnSync inherits process.env. GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN therefore become available to the Codex process, reversing the prior deliberate credential boundary; a prompt-driven agent or any tooling it launches can read and exfiltrate CI GitHub credentials.

findings.title: Restore the fork-PR guard before running untrusted code
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the head-repository check allows a fork PR to reach this self-hosted job. The workflow checks out the attacker-controlled head SHA and then runs its dependency installation and `src/cli.ts`, giving the fork author arbitrary command execution on the runner.

findings.title: Restore the fork guard before running PR code
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed condition previously limited this self-hosted job to same-repository PRs. Fork PRs now check out their attacker-controlled SHA and execute `pnpm install` and `tsx src/cli.ts` on the runner, permitting arbitrary code execution in the runner environment.

findings.title: Restore the same-repository gate for the self-hosted job
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the job-level condition makes pull requests from forks eligible for this self-hosted runner. The workflow checks out the fork-controlled head SHA, installs its dependency graph, and executes its fork-controlled src/cli.ts. A fork author can therefore run arbitrary commands on the runner and access any credentials, workspace state, or network privileges available to it.

findings.title: Preserve explicitly configured zero-duration timeouts
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, setting NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 or NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 produced an immediate next timeout stage. The new predicate silently replaces either valid configured value with 5000 ms or 2000 ms, respectively. Existing deployments that use zero to skip the grace or post-SIGKILL wait will now delay runner completion by seconds after upgrade.

findings.title: Preserve zero-valued shutdown durations
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 and NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 produced immediate setTimeout callbacks. This change instead silently substitutes 5000 ms and 2000 ms, respectively, so established deployments configured for immediate SIGKILL escalation or immediate completion after SIGKILL now wait 5 or 2 extra seconds.

findings.title: Preserve zero-valued runner grace intervals
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, both runner delay environment variables accepted `0`, enabling immediate SIGKILL escalation and immediate give-up after SIGKILL. They now silently fall back to 5000 ms and 2000 ms. A deployment that sets both to `0` can therefore wait an additional seven seconds after `invocation.timeoutMs` when an escaped descendant keeps pipes open.

findings.title: Carry deep-review residual risks into the critic
findings.whyItBreaks: Each deep review can report a blocking residual risk, but this replaces all of them with []. The critic therefore cannot distinguish a fully reviewed large PR from one with unresolved blocking evidence, and deriveVerdict can return a non-blocking result.

findings.title: Deep-review every changed file
findings.whyItBreaks: Large patches are limited to six selected hotspots. Removing the tail-coverage hotspot means any changed file absent from those six is never sent to deep.md; the critic receives only patchStat, not the skipped file's diff. A defect in such a file can therefore be reported as reviewed without any review pass inspecting it.

findings.title: Preserve distinct findings during deduplication
findings.whyItBreaks: The new key no longer includes whyItBreaks. Two independent defects reported against the same file/line/category with the same normalized 60-character title now collapse to one finding, even when their causes and fixes differ.

findings.title: Deep-review every changed file
findings.whyItBreaks: Only the six selected map hotspots are reviewed now. A changed file omitted by mapping, or one belonging only to a hotspot beyond MAX_HOTSPOTS, never reaches the deep-review loop. The critic receives only patchStat here, not the omitted diff, so it can return a clean review without examining that file.

findings.title: Pass deep-review residual risks to the critic
findings.whyItBreaks: Deep passes can report blocking residual risks, but this replacement always sends an empty residual_risks array to the critic. The final verdict is derived from the critic response, so an explicitly unresolved deep-review risk can be erased and the large PR reported as non-blocking.

findings.title: Restore coverage for unmapped changed files
findings.whyItBreaks: After selecting only the first six mapped hotspots, the removed coverage backstop no longer adds changed files absent from those hotspots. Those files receive no deep review; the critic receives only patchStat rather than their diff, so a large PR can return a completed/PASS review while changes in omitted files were never inspected.

findings.title: Preserve residual risks reported by deep passes
findings.whyItBreaks: Each successful deep pass can report residual risks, including blockers for incomplete evidence, but the merged candidate now replaces all of them with []. The critic is therefore told there are no residual risks and cannot preserve those blockers in its output; review() can expose an unblocked verdict despite a deep reviewer reporting unresolved risk.

findings.title: Preserve focus in large-review deep prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: The large-review path no longer replaces {{FOCUS}} in deep.md and no longer includes bundle.focus in the map input. A caller-supplied focus directive is therefore ignored for large patches (and the deep prompt receives the literal placeholder), while small patches still receive focus through the full bundle.

findings.title: Preserve focus when constructing large-review prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: The large-review path no longer replaces {{FOCUS}} with bundle.focus. Focused reviews that cross the large-patch threshold therefore send the literal placeholder to every deep pass instead of the user's requested scope, while small reviews still include focus through the full bundle.

findings.title: Preserve the requested focus for large reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: The large-review path now removes bundle.focus before the map pass and no longer substitutes it into each deep-review prompt. A focused review of a large patch therefore selects and evaluates hotspots without the requested scope; the deep prompt also retains its {{FOCUS}} placeholder instead of receiving the caller's value.

findings.title: Normalize rounded seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: For values in the final 500 ms of a minute, rounding the remainder produces 60 seconds after minutes have already been computed. For example, 59500 renders as "60s" instead of "1m 0s", and 119500 renders as "1m 60s" instead of "2m 0s". These values are rendered in review call and total-duration output.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into the minute component
findings.whyItBreaks: For 119500 ms, minutes is computed as 1 while seconds rounds from 59.5 to 60, so rendered review stats show "1m 60s" instead of the correct "2m 0s". Both per-call and total durations use this formatter.

findings.title: Normalize seconds rounding into the minute component
findings.whyItBreaks: For 119500 ms, minutes is floored to 1 while the remaining 59500 ms rounds to 60 seconds, so rendered review stats say "1m 60s" instead of the correctly rounded "2m 0s". The same boundary error occurs before every minute rollover.

findings.title: Reject zero to preserve the positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: `parsePositiveInteger("0", label)` now returns `0`, although both its exported name and its error contract promise a positive integer. Public callers can therefore receive an invalid zero value where they rely on values being greater than zero.

findings.title: Reject zero in parsePositiveInteger
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported function promises a positive integer (and retains that error text), but the changed predicate accepts "0" and returns 0. Callers may rely on this parser to enforce a strictly-positive option.

findings.title: Reject zero in the positive-integer parser
findings.whyItBreaks: parsePositiveInteger("0", label) now returns 0, although the exported function name and its error contract promise a positive integer. Callers can therefore receive an invalid zero value without an error.
